#### Low SI Dispersion ($m=15, s=3$)

```{r}
#| label: fig-low-dispersion-summary
#| fig-cap: "Simulation summary for N = 100 under low SI dispersion (m = 15, s = 3). The left and middle panels show SI mean and SD estimation biases for converged runs, while the right panel shows convergence percentages across all 100 repetitions. The iteration cap is 300."
#| echo: false
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(
  file.path(
    simulation_dir,
    "Combined_summary_panels",
    "Simu_results_s100_r100_i300_low_dispersion_mean_sd_convergence_large_text.pdf"
  )
)
```

Under low dispersion, the component distributions are relatively well separated, but performance depended heavily on the availability of direct primary-secondary (PS) information. In the baseline profile containing the highest PS proportion ($w_{\mathrm{PS}}=0.50$), the method achieved accurate parameter recovery, yielding a mean RMSE of 0.66 days and an SD RMSE of 0.43 days (@tbl-main-simulation). However, when the PS proportion was reduced to 0.35 in the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles, estimation accuracy deteriorated drastically (mean RMSE increased to 11.73 and 14.49 days, respectively). Notably, as shown in the top panel of the simulation summary (@fig-low-dispersion-summary), all three profiles achieved 100% numerical convergence within the 300-iteration limit. This contrast reveals a critical limitation: while a compact SI distribution provides favourable conditions for separating pathways, a lack of sufficient direct PS information can cause the algorithm to stably converge to highly inaccurate local optima. Thus, successful convergence does not guarantee accurate parameter recovery.

#### Moderate SI Dispersion ($m=2, s=2$)

```{r}
#| label: fig-moderate-dispersion-summary
#| fig-cap: "Simulation summary for N = 100 under moderate SI dispersion (m = 2, s = 2). The left and middle panels show SI mean and SD estimation biases for converged runs, while the right panel shows convergence percentages across all 100 repetitions. The iteration cap is 300."
#| echo: false
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(
  file.path(
    simulation_dir,
    "Combined_summary_panels",
    "Simu_results_s100_r100_i300_moderate_dispersion_mean_sd_convergence_large_text.pdf"
  )
)
```

As the underlying SI distribution widens and pathway components begin to overlap, the estimation dynamics change substantially. Under moderate dispersion, the absolute errors appeared smaller (mean RMSE 0.50 to 1.05 days; SD RMSE 0.84 to 0.93 days), but these deviations were substantial relative to the true SI mean and SD of 2 days (@tbl-main-simulation). While the baseline profile again produced the lowest mean RMSE, the method struggled to accurately recover SI variability across all transmission structures. Furthermore, the middle panel of the simulation summary (@fig-moderate-dispersion-summary) highlights a severe decline in algorithmic stability: convergence rates plummeted to 37%, 32%, and 24% for the baseline, CP-heavy, and higher-generation-heavy profiles, respectively. This suggests that moderate dispersion compromises the model's ability to confidently differentiate transmission pathways; a larger PS proportion is no longer sufficient to guarantee reliable convergence or highly accurate recovery within the iteration limit.

#### High SI Dispersion ($m=5, s=10$)

```{r}
#| label: fig-high-dispersion-summary
#| fig-cap: "Simulation summary for N = 100 under high SI dispersion (m = 5, s = 10). The left and middle panels show SI mean and SD estimation biases for converged runs, while the right panel shows convergence percentages across all 100 repetitions. The iteration cap is 300."
#| echo: false
#| fig-pos: "H"
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(
  file.path(
    simulation_dir,
    "Combined_summary_panels",
    "Simu_results_s100_r100_i300_high_dispersion_mean_sd_convergence_large_text.pdf"
  )
)
```

Under high dispersion, the extreme right-skew and massive overlap between pathway-specific distributions act as a stress test for the model. The bottom panel of the simulation summary (@fig-high-dispersion-summary) shows that the method demonstrated considerable difficulty in parameter recovery regardless of the underlying transmission structure. While mean RMSE ranged from 1.83 to 2.27 days, the model fundamentally failed to capture SI variability, producing SD RMSE values between 6.63 and 7.27 days against a true SD of 10 days (@tbl-main-simulation). Convergence rates also remained poor, ranging from 37% to 53%. In this scenario, the heavy overlap effectively obscures the true transmission links, making the contributions of different pathways practically indistinguishable. Consequently, the method proves unreliable for highly dispersed SI distributions, as altering the transmission pathway composition cannot compensate for the fundamental loss of parameter identifiability.



### Effect of sample size

As expected, larger sample sizes ($N=50, 100, 200$) generally reduced estimation error (RMSE) across most scenarios, particularly under moderate and high dispersion. However, larger samples did not consistently improve numerical convergence, with convergence rates declining across all three pathway profiles under moderate dispersion. Substantial estimation errors also persisted in the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles under low dispersion, despite increasing sample size. Detailed results are provided in Appendix C (@fig-sample-size-effect; @tbl-all-simulation-results).


### Investigation of anomalous SI estimates under low-dispersion scenario
Under low dispersion, estimation error was substantial despite consistently successful numerical convergence. This is partly expected, since the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles contain relatively few PS observations. However, the estimates were tightly clustered around incorrect values rather than widely dispersed, suggesting stable convergence to inaccurate solutions rather than imprecision alone. To investigate this phenomenon, we examined representative EM fitting trajectories for these non-baseline profiles. We found that initializing the EM algorithm with the empirical moments of the overall ICC dataset—whose variance substantially exceeded that of the true SI distribution—caused an early misallocation of latent pathway responsibilities. Because SI parameter updates depend entirely on these assigned responsibilities, the initial misallocation continuously reinforced biased parameter updates, driving the algorithm to satisfy its convergence criterion at estimates far from the true values. These findings indicate that the anomalous errors were primarily driven by EM initialization behaviour rather than the underlying SI distribution itself. For a detailed visual breakdown of how the EM algorithm dynamically shifts component weights and updates parameter estimates across successive iterations, see Appendix C.3.


## Sensitivity analysis

### Sensitivity to Initial Parameter Values

Building on the trajectory analysis findings, a targeted sensitivity analysis was conducted to systematically assess the impact of initial parameter values on estimation accuracy under the problematic low-dispersion scenarios. By comparing the default ICC-based initialization against alternative starting parameters, the analysis confirmed that the large biases observed in the non-baseline profiles were primarily driven by the inflated empirical ICC variance used during initialization. Supplying more appropriate starting values substantially improved parameter recovery and reduced estimation bias. This demonstrates that the severe inaccuracies observed earlier reflect the EM algorithm's general sensitivity to initial conditions, rather than a fundamental lack of identifiability within the Log-Normal extension itself. A complete breakdown of this sensitivity analysis, including the specific alternative initialization strategies evaluated, is provided in Appendix C.4.

## Data analysis

To evaluate the empirical performance of the Log-Normal extension, four historical scabies outbreak datasets were selected. First, previous analyses of these datasets under the Normal SI model by Ainslie et al. [@ainslie2025mitey] provide established reference estimates for direct comparison. Second, these datasets exhibit relatively low SI dispersion in relation to their estimated means, providing a useful setting for assessing the consistency of the Log-Normal extension under less extreme variability. Third, the studies cover diverse epidemiological settings, including a fishing community, a kindergarten, a preschool, and a care home, with differing observed ICC interval patterns. This allows the two distributional assumptions to be compared across varied outbreak settings. The fitted ICC mixture distributions are presented in @fig-scabies-model-overlay, with the corresponding SI parameter estimates summarised in @tbl-scabies-comparison.


![ICC distributions and fitted mixture densities for four scabies outbreak datasets: (A) Akunzirwe, (B) Ariza, (C) Kaburi, and (D) Tjon-Kon-Fat. The horizontal axis shows ICC interval (days) and the vertical axis shows density. Black bars represent the ICC intervals, while the red dashed and blue solid curves show the fitted Normal and Log-Normal mixture densities, respectively. The vertical black dashed line indicates the estimated SI mean under the Log-Normal model. The panels allow comparison of the two distributional assumptions against the ICC patterns.](<../Simulation_results/data_analysis_normal_lognormal_overlay.png>){#fig-scabies-model-overlay width="55%"}


| Study | Normal mean | Log-Normal mean | Normal SD | Log-Normal SD |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Akunzirwe | 122.9 | 125.4 | 26.9 | 31.0 |
| Ariza | 98.4 | 98.4 | 8.5 | 9.0 |
| Kaburi | 167.3 | 167.4 | 9.7 | 10.7 |
| Tjon-Kon-Fat | 110.7 | 112.3 | 16.1 | 15.2 |

: Comparison of estimated serial interval means and standard deviations (days) between the Normal and Log-Normal models across four scabies outbreak datasets. {#tbl-scabies-comparison}


@fig-scabies-model-overlay compares the fitted Normal and Log-Normal ICC mixture distributions across the four scabies datasets, while @tbl-scabies-comparison presents the corresponding SI parameter estimates. Across all four studies, the Log-Normal model produced SI means that were either identical to or slightly higher than those from the Normal model (e.g., increasing from 122.9 to 125.4 days in the Akunzirwe dataset; @tbl-scabies-comparison). This consistent tendency stems from the interaction between the Log-Normal distribution's shape and the EM algorithm's expectation (E) step. Because the Log-Normal distribution possesses a heavier right tail, it assigns higher posterior responsibilities to longer ICC intervals for the primary-secondary (PS) pathway. Consequently, these larger values pull the responsibility-weighted mean upward during the maximization (M) step, whereas the rapidly decaying tail of the Normal distribution forces the algorithm to reallocate these longer intervals to higher-generation pathways (PT or PQ).

The estimated SI standard deviation (SD) exhibited a diverging pattern depending on the dataset. In the first three outbreaks (Akunzirwe, Ariza, and Kaburi), the Log-Normal SD was larger than the Normal SD (@tbl-scabies-comparison). This general increase aligns with theoretical expectations: by absorbing more right-tail ICC observations into the PS component, the Log-Normal model inherently broadens its variance to accommodate these dispersed values. This is particularly evident in the Akunzirwe dataset (Panel A of @fig-scabies-model-overlay), where heterogeneous community-wide transmission naturally produced a highly dispersed distribution of symptom onset times, leading to a substantial SD increase from 26.9 to 31.0 days (@tbl-scabies-comparison).

Conversely, for the Tjon-Kon-Fat et al. dataset (Panel D of @fig-scabies-model-overlay), the Log-Normal SD decreased from 16.1 to 15.2 days (@tbl-scabies-comparison). This anomaly highlights how specific epidemiological settings interact with algorithmic pathway allocation. Unlike the open community in Akunzirwe, the Tjon-Kon-Fat outbreak occurred in a highly monitored care home. Rapid interventions in such institutional settings likely truncated prolonged transmission chains, resulting in a tightly concentrated ICC peak with no pronounced right tail. Faced with this compact data structure, the inherently right-skewed Log-Normal distribution is forced to shrink its PS variance to accurately fit the sharp main peak, shedding the remaining edge observations to the CP or PT/PQ pathways during the E-step. In contrast, the symmetric Normal distribution accommodates these minor edge variations by simply inflating its overall variance, resulting in a comparatively larger SD.

Taken together, @fig-scabies-model-overlay and @tbl-scabies-comparison demonstrate that the Log-Normal extension produces SI parameter estimates broadly consistent with those obtained under the established Normal model. The relatively small differences between the two models may reflect the low relative dispersion of these scabies datasets, which may not fully reveal the potential advantages of the Log-Normal assumption. Nevertheless, the Log-Normal model provides greater flexibility in representing positive, right-skewed SI distributions, with differences in the fitted mixture curves and slightly larger estimated SDs in three of the four studies. These findings support the practical feasibility of the Log-Normal extension, while its potential benefits for more strongly right-skewed SI distributions remain to be investigated.


# Software Implementation


## Package Context and Purpose

The proposed Log-Normal extension was implemented within the existing `{mitey}` R package [@ainslie2025mitey], originally developed to support serial-interval estimation and reproduction-number analysis from infectious-disease outbreak data. The package has two main functions: estimating the mean and standard deviation of the serial interval (SI) from index-case-to-case (ICC) intervals using the transmission-pathway framework of Vink et al. [@vink2014], and estimating the time-varying reproduction number using the Wallinga–Lipsitch method where the reproduction number relies on an estimate of the serial interval. This project focuses exclusively on extending the SI estimation component, leaving the reproduction-number functionality unchanged.

The original `si_estim()` function supports Normal and Gamma assumptions for the underlying SI distribution. This project introduces a Log-Normal option to accommodate right-skewed SI distributions. The extension provides greater flexibility in selecting an appropriate distributional assumption while preserving the original workflow.


## Extensions to the `{mitey}` Package

The Log-Normal option was integrated using the pathway-specific distributional approximations and discretised likelihood described in Sections 3.1.3–3.1.4 (summarised in @tbl-path-summary), together with the adapted EM estimation procedure described in Section 3.2 (@fig-em-Log-Normal). This involved adapting the component-density calculations, posterior pathway responsibilities, and SI parameter updates, together with handling zero-day ICC observations and assessing numerical convergence. Further mathematical and computational details of the EM updates, zero-day handling, and convergence criteria are provided in Appendix A, while the accuracy of the pathway-specific approximations is examined in Appendix B.

## Code and Data Availability

The source code for the Log-Normal extension, together with the simulation scripts and results, is available in the [`terry` development branch](https://github.com/kylieainslie/mitey/tree/terry) of the `{mitey}` R package. The historical scabies ICC data used in the empirical analysis are available in the same repository ([`si_data.rds`](https://github.com/kylieainslie/mitey/blob/terry/inst/extdata/data/si_data.rds)).



# Discussion

This study extended the transmission-pathway mixture framework of Vink et al. [@vink2014] by introducing a Log-Normal assumption for the underlying serial interval (SI) distribution. Three principal findings emerged. First, under low dispersion, accurate parameter recovery was achieved in the baseline profile, but substantial biases occurred under alternative pathway compositions despite successful numerical convergence. Second, under moderate and high dispersion, greater overlap between pathway distributions was associated with poorer parameter recovery, particularly for SI variability, and lower convergence rates within the prescribed iteration limit. Increasing sample size did not consistently resolve these difficulties. Third, application to four historical scabies datasets yielded SI estimates broadly consistent with those obtained under the Normal model. Together, these findings support the feasibility of the Log-Normal extension while highlighting the importance of transmission structure and numerical estimation behaviour.

The simulation results further revealed that numerical convergence does not necessarily guarantee accurate parameter recovery. Under low dispersion, the baseline profile achieved RMSEs of 0.66 and 0.43 days for the SI mean and standard deviation, respectively, whereas the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles exhibited substantial biases despite 100% convergence (@tbl-main-simulation; @fig-low-dispersion-summary). Additional investigations suggested that initialization could influence posterior pathway responsibilities and lead to inaccurate estimates even after numerical convergence (@fig-em-trajectory; @fig-init-sensitivity). Under greater dispersion, increased pathway overlap may further complicate the allocation of ICC observations to latent transmission routes, particularly the primary-secondary (PS) component used for SI parameter updates. Allowing more EM iterations improved convergence in supplementary analyses, but did not establish that parameter recovery was reliable. Since RMSE was calculated only from converged runs, estimation accuracy should be interpreted alongside convergence rates. These findings suggest that pathway overlap, initialization sensitivity, and computational constraints may jointly affect estimation performance.

Previous studies have explored different distributional assumptions and transmission structures for serial-interval estimation. Vink et al. [@vink2014] developed a four-pathway ICC mixture model using a Normal SI distribution, with Gamma considered as an alternative. Ainslie et al. [@ainslie2025] subsequently applied this framework to scabies outbreaks, finding poorer visual fit under the Gamma assumption. Meanwhile, Nishiura et al. [@nishiura2020] identified Log-Normal as the best-fitting candidate distribution for early COVID-19 transmission-pair data. Our study extends the Vink framework to a Log-Normal SI distribution when transmission links are unknown. Applied to the same four scabies datasets, it produced estimates broadly consistent with those of Ainslie et al., although superior fit or accuracy was not established (@tbl-scabies-comparison). In contrast, Stockdale et al. [@stockdale2023] adopted a Gamma-based mixture model that allows an arbitrary number of unobserved intermediate cases, using genomic and symptom-onset data to infer possible transmission networks. While our approach requires only symptom-onset data, it retains the four-pathway restriction, which may limit its applicability to longer or more complex transmission chains.

These comparisons highlight both the strengths and limitations of the present study. A key strength is its systematic evaluation across different SI dispersion levels, transmission structures, and sample sizes, supported by additional investigations of initialization and numerical convergence. Its implementation within the {mitey} R package also provides a basis for further methodological development. However, two main limitations remain. First, the framework is restricted to four transmission pathways, which may not adequately represent longer or more complex transmission chains. Second, under moderate or high SI dispersion, substantial overlap between pathway-specific ICC distributions may make it difficult to distinguish the contributions of different transmission routes and reliably recover the underlying SI parameters. This presents a challenge to practical identifiability that cannot necessarily be resolved by better initialization or additional EM iterations.

These findings have several practical implications. Researchers should consider the epidemiological characteristics of the disease when selecting an SI distribution, particularly whether negative intervals are plausible and whether strong right-skewness is expected. The availability of direct transmission information and the extent of overlap between transmission pathways should also be considered when interpreting estimates. In practice, examining multiple initial values, allowing sufficient EM iterations, and assessing the stability of parameter estimates may help identify numerical difficulties. Future research could develop more robust initialization strategies and model-comparison procedures, investigate parameter identifiability and alternative observation mechanisms, and extend the framework to additional transmission pathways. Exploring other flexible distributions, such as Weibull and generalised Gamma distributions, may further broaden its applicability.

Overall, this study demonstrates that the Log-Normal extension can achieve accurate SI parameter recovery under favourable conditions, particularly under low dispersion with sufficient direct PS information. Through simulation studies across different SI dispersion levels and transmission-pathway compositions, we also identified scenarios where parameter recovery and numerical convergence were less reliable. Its application to four historical scabies datasets produced estimates broadly consistent with those obtained under the Normal model. The Log-Normal distribution may provide a more appropriate representation of right-skewed SI distributions with long right tails. Further empirical analyses beyond the scabies datasets, particularly for diseases with more pronounced SI skewness, are needed to evaluate its potential advantages over the Normal model.

# Appendix

## Appendix A. Additional Details of the EM Estimation Procedure

This appendix provides the mathematical updates and numerical details underlying the EM procedure described in the Methods section. The four transmission pathways, their Log-Normal working densities, and the triangular discretisation of ICC intervals are defined in the main text and are not repeated here. The additional details concern latent pathway responsibilities, PS-weighted parameter updates, zero-day observations, and convergence assessment.

### A.1 Latent Pathway Responsibilities and the Vink Updating Principle

Throughout this Appendix, $N$ is the number of ICC observations, $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ indexes observations, $g$ and $h$ index pathways in $\mathcal G$, and $r=0,1,2,\ldots$ indexes EM iterations. The vector $\mathbf w=(w_g:g\in\mathcal G)$ contains the four pathway weights.

Let $T_i=t_i$ denote the observed integer-day ICC interval for observation $i$, and let $Z_i\in\mathcal G=\{\mathrm{CP},\mathrm{PS},\mathrm{PT},\mathrm{PQ}\}$ denote its unobserved transmission pathway. Define the latent indicator $z_{ig}$, which records whether observation $i$ belongs to pathway $g$:

$$
z_{ig}=\begin{cases}
1,&Z_i=g,\\
0,&Z_i\neq g.
\end{cases}
$$

If the pathway labels were observed, the complete-data log-likelihood associated with pathway membership would be

$$
\ell_c(m,s,\mathbf w)
=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}
z_{ig}\left\{\log w_g+\log p_{ig}(m,s)\right\},
$$

where $\ell_c$ denotes the complete-data log-likelihood, the subscript $c$ denotes “complete data”, $m$ and $s$ denote the natural-scale SI mean and SD, $w_g$ is the mixture weight of pathway $g$, and $p_{ig}(m,s)$ is the discretised probability of observation $i$ under pathway $g$. The logarithm is the natural logarithm, and the two summation signs combine contributions over all observations and pathways.

At iteration $r$, the E-step replaces the unobserved indicators with the posterior responsibilities $\tau_{ig}^{(r)}$, the conditional probability that pathway $g$ generated observation $i$ under the current parameter values:

$$
\tau_{ig}^{(r)}
=\operatorname{Pr}(Z_i=g\mid T_i=t_i,\mathbf w^{(r)},m^{(r)},s^{(r)})
=\frac{w_g^{(r)}p_{ig}(m^{(r)},s^{(r)})}
{\displaystyle\sum_{h\in\mathcal G}w_h^{(r)}p_{ih}(m^{(r)},s^{(r)})}.
$$

In the denominator, $h$ is a dummy pathway index used to sum over all four possible pathways. The responsibilities satisfy $\sum_g\tau_{ig}^{(r)}=1$ for each observation and provide fractional rather than deterministic pathway assignments. Their average updates the pathway proportions:

$$
w_g^{(r+1)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_{ig}^{(r)}.
$$

The current weights must enter each E-step because pathway prevalence influences the posterior assignments. Importantly, all four pathways contribute to this weight update, whereas the parameters of the underlying SI distribution are updated using the primary-secondary (PS) responsibilities only. In the original Normal version of the Vink procedure [@vink2014], $\mu^{(r+1)}$ and $(\sigma^2)^{(r+1)}$ denote the updated natural-scale SI mean and variance. Their corresponding PS-weighted updates were

$$
\mu^{(r+1)}
=\frac{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}t_i}
{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}},
\qquad
(\sigma^2)^{(r+1)}
=\frac{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}
(t_i-\mu^{(r+1)})^2}
{\sum_i\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}}.
$$

In these expressions, each unbounded sum over $i$ runs over all $N$ observations. The expressions are included for comparison: the Log-Normal extension retains the PS-only updating principle but changes the scale on which the SI moments are calculated.

### A.2 PS-Weighted Updates Under the Log-Normal SI Model

For the Log-Normal extension, write $\log X\sim N(\eta,\zeta^2)$ for a direct SI $X$, where $\eta$ and $\zeta^2$ are the mean and variance of the log-transformed SI. Let $a_i^{(r)}=\tau_{i,\mathrm{PS}}^{(r)}$ be observation $i$'s PS responsibility, and define $Y_i=\log T_i^*$ as its zero-safe log interval, where $T_i^*$ is the zero-safe M-step value described below. Set

$$
A_1^{(r)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i^{(r)},
\qquad
A_2^{(r)}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(a_i^{(r)}\right)^2.
$$

Thus, $A_1^{(r)}$ is the total PS responsibility at iteration $r$, while $A_2^{(r)}$ is the sum of squared PS responsibilities used in the finite-sample correction.

The responsibility-weighted log-scale mean and variance are updated by

$$
\eta^{(r+1)}
=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i^{(r)}Y_i}
{A_1^{(r)}},
$$

$$
(\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}
=\frac{A_1^{(r)}}{\left(A_1^{(r)}\right)^2-A_2^{(r)}}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_i^{(r)}
\left(Y_i-\eta^{(r+1)}\right)^2.
$$

The second expression is the finite-sample-corrected weighted variance used in the implementation; it is distinct from the uncorrected weighted variance commonly used in a likelihood M-step. The estimates are transformed back to the natural scale as follows, where $\exp(\cdot)$ denotes the exponential function:

$$
m^{(r+1)}
=\exp\left(\eta^{(r+1)}+\frac{(\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}}{2}\right),
$$

$$
s^{(r+1)}
=\sqrt{\left\{\exp\big((\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}\big)-1\right\}
\exp\left\{2\eta^{(r+1)}+(\zeta^2)^{(r+1)}\right\}}.
$$

The PS component represents a single direct SI and therefore follows the target Log-Normal distribution without an additional pathway-density approximation. Restricting the parameter updates to observations weighted by their PS responsibilities limits the direct influence of CP observations and longer-generation PT/PQ intervals. These other pathways still affect the estimates indirectly through their contributions to the E-step denominator and the subsequent PS responsibilities. In particular, misallocation of higher-generation observations to PS can influence the SI estimates despite the PS-only update.

Because this implementation uses corrected responsibility-weighted moments of discretised ICC values rather than an exact maximisation of the full interval-censored mixture likelihood, it should be understood as a Vink-style EM updating procedure rather than a guarantee of monotonic improvement in the full observed-data likelihood.

### A.3 Treatment of Zero-Day ICC Intervals

Zero-day ICC intervals represent valid observations in which cases have symptom onset recorded on the same day. However, extending the Vink updating procedure to a Log-Normal SI distribution introduces a numerical difficulty because the M-step operates on logarithmically transformed intervals, for which

$$
\log(0)=-\infty.
$$

A naive approach would be to replace zero with a very small positive value. However, this produces an extremely negative log observation. If the corresponding interval receives non-negligible PS responsibility, it may pull the estimated log-scale mean downward and substantially inflate the log-scale variance. The resulting PS density becomes more dispersed, potentially altering the posterior responsibilities calculated in subsequent E-steps. These changes may, in turn, further distort the parameter updates, creating a positive-feedback mechanism:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_i=0
&\longrightarrow \text{extreme negative log value}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{inflated log-scale variance}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{overly dispersed PS density}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{distorted PS responsibilities}\\
&\longrightarrow \text{potential further variance inflation}.
\end{aligned}
$$

To avoid this numerical instability, an **E/M-decoupled zero-handling strategy** was implemented. In the E-step, the original zero-day observation is retained when evaluating the pathway-specific discretised likelihood. In the current implementation, its contribution is calculated as

$$
p_g^{\mathrm{impl}}(0;m,s)
=
\int_0^1 2(1-c)f_g(c;m,s)\,dc.
$$

Here, $p_g^{\mathrm{impl}}(0;m,s)$ is the implemented probability assigned to a zero-day observation under pathway $g$, the superscript “impl” distinguishes this implementation-specific expression from the general discretisation formula, $f_g(c;m,s)$ is pathway $g$'s continuous ICC density at $c$, and $m,s$ are the natural-scale SI mean and SD.

Only during the logarithmic M-step is a separate zero-safe working value introduced:

$$
T_i^*=
\begin{cases}
1, & T_i=0,\\
T_i, & T_i>0,
\end{cases}
\qquad
Y_i=\log(T_i^*).
$$

Thus, a zero-day observation contributes $Y_i=0$ to the responsibility-weighted log-scale parameter updates, avoiding the extreme negative log values that could otherwise destabilise estimation. The replacement value of one is a computational proxy rather than an assumption that the underlying continuous ICC interval lasted exactly one day.

This separation retains the observed zero-day interval during pathway classification while preventing the logarithmic singularity from entering the M-step. Although the proxy does not constitute an exact treatment of interval censoring in the parameter update, it provides a numerically stable implementation of the PS-weighted updating procedure.

### A.4 Initialization and Joint Convergence Criterion

The implementation begins with initial natural-scale SI parameters $(m^{(0)},s^{(0)})$ and equal initial pathway weights $w_g^{(0)}=1/4$. Unless alternative starting parameters are supplied, the initial mean and SD are obtained from the empirical ICC intervals. The sensitivity analysis in the Results section examines the effect of varying these initial values while keeping the ICC datasets fixed.

At iteration $r$, the stopping rule monitors relative changes in the natural-scale SI parameters and the largest absolute change in the four mixture weights:

$$
\Delta_m^{(r)}
=\frac{|m^{(r+1)}-m^{(r)}|}{|m^{(r)}|+\epsilon},
\qquad
\Delta_s^{(r)}
=\frac{|s^{(r+1)}-s^{(r)}|}{|s^{(r)}|+\epsilon},
$$

$$
\Delta_w^{(r)}
=\max_{g\in\mathcal G}\left|w_g^{(r+1)}-w_g^{(r)}\right|,
$$

Here, $\Delta_m^{(r)}$ and $\Delta_s^{(r)}$ are the relative changes in the natural-scale SI mean and SD, $\Delta_w^{(r)}$ is the largest absolute change among the four weights, and $\epsilon$ is a small positive constant that prevents division by zero. Numerical convergence is declared only when

$$
\Delta_m^{(r)}<\mathrm{tol},\qquad
\Delta_s^{(r)}<\mathrm{tol},\qquad
\Delta_w^{(r)}<\mathrm{tol}.
$$

The symbol $\mathrm{tol}$ denotes the positive convergence tolerance, whose default value is $10^{-6}$. Joint monitoring prevents termination based only on apparently stable SI parameters while pathway weights are still changing. The simulation analyses imposed a maximum of 300 iterations. Nevertheless, satisfying this stopping rule indicates numerical stability of the updates, not necessarily accurate recovery of the generating SI parameters, as demonstrated by the low-dispersion simulation and initialization sensitivity results.


## Appendix B. Assessment of Component-Density Approximations

The Log-Normal extension uses computationally tractable working densities for the co-primary (CP), primary-tertiary (PT), and primary-quaternary (PQ) transmission pathways. As described in the Methods section, the ideal CP interval is the absolute difference of two independent Log-Normal serial intervals, whereas PT and PQ are sums of two and three independent intervals, respectively. The PS pathway comprises one direct serial interval and is represented exactly.

This appendix evaluates how closely these working densities approximate their ideal continuous distributions. The assessment concerns distributional approximation rather than bias in estimated SI parameters or the additional effects of rounding ICC intervals to calendar days.

### B.1 Co-primary pathway: Half-Normal approximation

Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ denote independent serial intervals following the same Log-Normal distribution with natural-scale mean $m$ and standard deviation $s$. The exact co-primary interval is $C_{\mathrm{CP}}=|X_1-X_2|$. Writing $f_X$ for the density of one SI, its exact continuous density can be expressed as

$$
f_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(c)
=
2\int_0^\infty f_X(x)f_X(x+c)\,dx,
\qquad c\geq 0.
$$

The working model approximates the signed difference $X_1-X_2$ by a Normal distribution with mean zero and variance $2s^2$, giving the Half-Normal density

$$
f_{\mathrm{CP}}^{\mathrm{HN}}(c)
=
\frac{1}{s\sqrt{\pi}}
\exp\left(-\frac{c^2}{4s^2}\right),
\qquad c\geq 0.
$$

This approximation preserves the variance scale of the signed difference before taking its absolute value, but does not necessarily reproduce the moments or shape of the exact CP distribution. In particular, the exact density depends on both $m$ and $s$, whereas the Half-Normal approximation depends only on $s$. Differences in concentration near zero, curvature, and tail behaviour may therefore arise, especially when the underlying SI distribution is highly dispersed and right-skewed.

### B.2 PT and PQ pathways: Distributional cost of the Fenton--Wilkinson approximation

The Fenton--Wilkinson (FW) approximation replaces a sum of independent Log-Normal serial intervals with a single Log-Normal distribution matching its exact natural-scale mean and variance.

For $S_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}X_j$, the exact moments are $E(S_n)=nm$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=ns^2$, where $n=2$ for PT and $n=3$ for PQ. Although the FW approximation preserves these two moments, it does not necessarily reproduce higher-order distributional characteristics, particularly skewness.

Let

$$
c_v=\frac{s}{m}
$$

denote the coefficient of variation of the underlying SI distribution.

The skewness of a single Log-Normal variable is $(c_v^2+3)c_v$. Since the serial intervals are independent, the skewness of their sum is

$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{sum},n}
=
\frac{(c_v^2+3)c_v}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

The moment-matched FW distribution has coefficient of variation $c_v/\sqrt{n}$. Its skewness is therefore

$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{FW},n}
=
\frac{(c_v^2/n+3)c_v}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

The resulting skewness difference is

$$
\Delta\gamma_n
=
\gamma_{\mathrm{sum},n}
-
\gamma_{\mathrm{FW},n}
=
\frac{c_v^3(1-1/n)}{\sqrt{n}},
\qquad n>1.
$$

Because $\Delta\gamma_n>0$, the FW approximation has lower overall positive skewness than the exact sum. The discrepancy increases with $c_v^3$, suggesting that the approximation becomes less accurate as the underlying SI distribution becomes more variable and strongly right-skewed.

Importantly, this result concerns the standardised third moment. It does not imply that the FW density is lower than the exact density at every point in the right tail.

### B.3 Numerical assessment of approximation accuracy

To assess the magnitude of these distributional discrepancies, the ideal and working pathway-specific densities were compared under the three SI settings used in the main simulation: low dispersion $(m,s)=(15,3)$, moderate dispersion $(2,2)$, and high dispersion $(5,10)$.

For CP, the exact absolute-difference density was evaluated numerically and compared with its Half-Normal approximation. For PT and PQ, exact sums of independent Log-Normal intervals were evaluated using numerical convolution and compared with their FW approximations.

The accuracy of each approximation was quantified using the density overlap coefficient,

$$
\operatorname{OVL}(f,g)
=
\int_0^\infty
\min\{f(c),g(c)\}\,dc
=
1-\frac{1}{2}
\int_0^\infty |f(c)-g(c)|\,dc.
$$

Values closer to 100% indicate greater agreement between the two continuous densities.

![Comparison of ideal and working pathway-specific ICC densities under three Log-Normal SI dispersion settings. Rows represent low ($m=15$, $s=3$), moderate ($m=2$, $s=2$), and high ($m=5$, $s=10$) dispersion; columns correspond to CP, PS, PT, and PQ pathways. The horizontal axis shows ICC interval (days) and the vertical axis shows density. Solid dark curves represent the ideal continuous distributions, while dashed orange curves represent the working approximations; shaded regions indicate differences between them. CP uses a Half-Normal approximation to the absolute difference of two independent Log-Normal intervals, PS is exact, and PT/PQ use Fenton--Wilkinson approximations. Panel annotations report density overlap percentages calculated over the full numerical domain. Comparisons precede calendar-day discretisation. In the main simulation, CP observations were generated using the Half-Normal working model rather than the exact Log-Normal difference distribution.](../Simulation_results/component_approximation_comparison_corrected.png){#fig-component-approximation width="100%"}

As shown in @fig-component-approximation, the working densities closely approximate their ideal counterparts under low SI dispersion. The density overlaps are approximately 98.24% for CP, 99.97% for PT, and 99.96% for PQ, while the PS component is represented exactly.

As shown in @fig-component-approximation, the discrepancies become more pronounced as dispersion increases. Under moderate dispersion, CP overlap decreases to approximately 77.51%, compared with 98.42% and 97.99% for PT and PQ. Under high dispersion, CP overlap decreases further to approximately 58.81%, whereas PT and PQ retain overlaps of approximately 95.88% and 94.40%, respectively.

The numerical comparisons in @fig-component-approximation are consistent with the theoretical expectations. The increasingly large FW skewness gap is reflected in declining density overlap under higher dispersion, although the overall PT/PQ approximations remain relatively close. In contrast, the Half-Normal approximation can differ substantially from the exact CP density, particularly near zero.

The results in @fig-component-approximation indicate that approximation accuracy depends on the underlying SI dispersion and transmission pathway. However, density overlap does not directly quantify bias in EM-based SI estimation. The effect of approximation error on estimated parameters also depends on pathway weights, discretised likelihood contributions, and posterior pathway responsibilities.

Furthermore, because the main simulation generated CP observations using the Half-Normal working model, it did not separately assess the additional parameter-estimation error that might arise when real CP intervals follow the exact absolute difference of independent Log-Normal serial intervals.


## Appendix C. Supplementary Simulation Results

### C.1 Effect of Sample Size

To investigate the influence of data availability, estimation performance was compared across four sample sizes ($N=20$, $50$, $100$, and $200$), while retaining the same nine combinations of SI dispersion and transmission structure. The resulting trends are shown in @fig-sample-size-effect, with the complete numerical results reported in @tbl-all-simulation-results.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sample-size-effect
#| fig-cap: "Effect of ICC sample size on parameter recovery and EM convergence. The horizontal axis gives sample size (20, 50, 100, 200); columns show low, moderate, and high SI dispersion, while rows show mean RMSE (days), SD RMSE (days), and convergence percentage. Colours identify the three pathway profiles. RMSE uses finite estimates from converged runs only; convergence uses all 100 repetitions per scenario. The EM iteration cap is 300. Compare how error and convergence change with sample size within each profile."
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "100%"

# Create this file once by running the separate plot_sample_size_effect.R script.
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(
  simulation_dir,
  "sample_size_effect_rmse_convergence_large_text.pdf"
))
```


As shown in @fig-sample-size-effect, increasing sample size tended to reduce RMSE, particularly under moderate and high dispersion, indicating that the SI parameter estimates from successfully converged runs generally became closer to their true values as more ICC observations were available. Under moderate dispersion, both mean and SD RMSE generally decreased as more ICC observations became available, although the reductions were relatively modest compared with those under high dispersion. Under high dispersion, estimation errors also decreased across all three pathway profiles, with the largest improvements generally occurring between $N=20$ and $N=50$.

However, the trends in @fig-sample-size-effect were not consistent across all scenarios. Under low dispersion, the baseline profile showed substantial reductions in both mean and SD RMSE as sample size increased. In contrast, the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles continued to exhibit large mean RMSE values, with little improvement as $N$ increased. In particular, the higher-generation-heavy profile maintained a mean RMSE of approximately 14–15 days across all four sample sizes, indicating a root-mean-squared estimation error comparable to the true SI mean of 15 days. Its SD RMSE also remained around 11 days, substantially exceeding the true SD of 3 days. These persistent errors suggest that increasing the sample size alone did not substantially improve parameter recovery in this scenario and may not resolve certain systematic estimation difficulties.

The relationship between sample size and convergence was more complex in @fig-sample-size-effect. Under low dispersion, convergence rates improved with increasing sample size and reached 100% for all three pathway profiles at $N=100$ and $N=200$. In contrast, under moderate dispersion, convergence rates consistently declined as sample size increased. For the baseline, CP-heavy, and higher-generation-heavy profiles, convergence decreased from 54%, 66%, and 68% at $N=20$ to 23%, 20%, and 9% at $N=200$, respectively. Under high dispersion, convergence patterns varied by transmission structure: the baseline and CP-heavy profiles fluctuated without a clear improvement, while the higher-generation-heavy profile showed a declining trend.

Taken together, @fig-sample-size-effect and @tbl-all-simulation-results indicate that larger sample sizes generally improve estimation accuracy in several scenarios, but do not necessarily lead to more reliable numerical convergence. In particular, the declining convergence rates under moderate dispersion, despite generally decreasing RMSE, suggest that estimation accuracy and convergence behaviour should be evaluated separately. Furthermore, the persistent estimation errors observed in some low-dispersion profiles indicate that certain limitations may not be overcome simply by increasing the amount of available ICC data.

### C.3 Investigation of anomalous SI estimates under low-dispersion scenario

An unexpected finding from the main simulation was the substantial estimation error under low dispersion, despite consistently successful numerical convergence (@tbl-main-simulation; @fig-low-dispersion-summary). At $N=100$, all three pathway profiles achieved 100% convergence, yet the SI mean RMSE reached 11.73 and 14.49 days under the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles, respectively. The simulation summary plot also showed that the estimates were relatively tightly clustered around values substantially different from the true parameters. This suggests that the large errors were not simply due to high variability across repetitions, but reflected a tendency towards stable yet inaccurate estimates.

To investigate how these inaccurate estimates arose, @fig-em-trajectory presents representative EM fitting trajectories for the two non-baseline profiles, showing the evolution of the fitted mixture density, SI parameters, and pathway weights across iterations.

![Representative EM trajectories under low SI dispersion ($m=15$, $s=3$) for one CP-heavy and one higher-generation-heavy repetition ($N=100$), each initialized from empirical ICC moments. Columns show iterations 0, 10, 30, and the converged fit. The horizontal axis is ICC interval (days) and the vertical axis is density. Light-blue bars show the same ICC intervals throughout each row; coloured curves show weighted CP, PS, PT, and PQ densities, the black curve is their fitted mixture, and the grey dashed curve is the working mixture at the true parameters. Grey and orange vertical lines mark the true and estimated SI means. Compare how component weights and the estimated mean move across iterations.](<../Simulation_results/EM_low_dispersion_static_snapshots_large_text.pdf>){#fig-em-trajectory width="100%"}

In the CP-heavy trajectory in @fig-em-trajectory, the estimated SI mean progressively decreased from 15.49 to 3.64 days, moving substantially away from the true value of 15 days. At the same time, the estimated CP weight approached zero, while the PQ weight increased to approximately 0.73. Notably, although the initial mean was close to the true SI mean, the initial SD was considerably larger than the true value (13.73 versus 3 days). This illustrates how an initially inaccurate representation of SI variability may be associated with changes in pathway allocation and subsequent parameter estimates.

In the higher-generation-heavy trajectory in @fig-em-trajectory, a different pattern emerged. The estimated SI mean increased from 24.95 to 27.84 days, while the PS weight progressively increased to approximately 0.75 and the PT and PQ weights approached zero. In this case, both the initial mean and SD were substantially larger than their true values. As the algorithm proceeded, an increasing proportion of observations was assigned to the PS component, resulting in an estimated SI distribution that differed considerably from the underlying distribution used for data generation.

The trajectories in @fig-em-trajectory suggest that the EM procedure can converge to substantially different parameter estimates through changes in the allocation of observations among latent pathways. Because the estimation of SI parameters depends on the posterior responsibilities assigned to the PS component, inaccurate pathway allocation may reinforce subsequent parameter updates, allowing the algorithm to stabilise at estimates far from the true values. Importantly, satisfying the numerical convergence criterion indicates that successive parameter updates have become sufficiently small; it does not establish that the recovered parameters are accurate.

The results therefore raise the possibility that the large estimation errors observed under low dispersion are partly associated with the initialization and numerical behaviour of the estimation procedure, rather than being an unavoidable consequence of the underlying SI distribution or transmission structure. This motivated the following sensitivity analysis, which investigates whether alternative initial parameter values can improve recovery of the true SI parameters.

### C.4 Sensitivity to Initial Parameter Values

The main simulation study revealed an unexpected pattern under the low-dispersion setting, where the true serial interval (SI) mean and standard deviation were 15 and 3 days, respectively (@tbl-main-simulation; @fig-low-dispersion-summary). Although the proposed EM algorithm recovered the underlying SI parameters accurately under the baseline transmission-pathway profile, it produced substantially biased estimates under the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles. In particular, the estimated SI means were consistently much lower or higher than the true value, even when the numerical convergence criterion was satisfied. This suggested that convergence of the iterative procedure did not necessarily imply accurate parameter recovery and motivated further investigation into the possible sources of these discrepancies.

One potential explanation was the choice of initial parameter values supplied to the EM algorithm. In the main simulation, the initial SI mean and standard deviation were taken directly from the empirical ICC intervals. However, because the ICC distribution is a mixture of four transmission pathways, its overall variability does not necessarily reflect that of the underlying SI distribution. Under low dispersion, the sample SD of the ICC intervals was substantially larger than the true SI SD in the representative trajectories shown in @fig-em-trajectory, potentially affecting the initial component densities and subsequent posterior pathway responsibilities. Preliminary numerical comparisons in @fig-init-sensitivity also suggested that changing the initial parameters, particularly the SD, could lead to substantially different final estimates.

To examine this possibility more systematically, a targeted sensitivity analysis was conducted under the low-dispersion setting. Three transmission-pathway profiles were retained: baseline, CP-heavy, and higher-generation-heavy. For each profile, 100 independent ICC datasets were generated with a sample size of $N=100$. Each dataset was then fitted using three combinations of initial SI mean and SD. The generating parameter values were used to hold one initial parameter fixed while varying the other, allowing the influence of each initial parameter on the final estimates to be examined separately.

1. **Mean-misspecified:** The initial mean was replaced by the empirical ICC sample mean, while the initial SD remained at its true value, $(m_0,s_0)=(\bar{T},s)$. This isolates the effect of using an ICC-derived initial mean.

2. **SD-misspecified:** The initial mean was fixed at its true value, while the initial SD was replaced by the empirical ICC sample SD, $(m_0,s_0)=(m,s_T)$. This isolates the effect of using an ICC-derived initial SD.

3. **ICC-based:** Both parameters were initialized using the empirical mean and SD of the ICC intervals, $(m_0,s_0)=(\bar{T},s_T)$. This reproduces the initialization approach adopted in the main simulation.

Here, $m_0$ and $s_0$ are the initial SI mean and SD supplied to the EM algorithm, while $\bar{T}$ and $s_T$ denote the sample mean and SD of the simulated ICC observations. Importantly, the same ICC dataset was fitted under all three initialization strategies within each repetition, allowing direct comparisons without additional variation from generating different samples. The maximum number of EM iterations was set to 300, with the convergence tolerance unchanged.

![Sensitivity to three EM initialization strategies under low SI dispersion ($m=15$, $s=3$; $N=100$; 100 repetitions per profile). Rows show baseline, CP-heavy, and higher-generation-heavy profiles; colours denote mean-misspecified, SD-misspecified, and ICC-based starts. The first two columns plot estimated minus true SI mean and SD (days): dots are repetitions, boxes show interquartile ranges, whiskers span the 5th--95th percentiles, and red dashed lines mark zero bias. The third column shows median EM iterations with interquartile-range bars; 'cap' counts runs reaching the 300-iteration limit. This diagnostic includes capped fits. The SD-bias axis is restricted for readability, excluding one extreme point from view while retaining it in summaries. Compare which initial parameter drives bias and computational effort.](<../Simulation_results/Init_sensitivity/Init_sensitivity_3x3_Bias_three_starts_iteration_boxplot.png>){#fig-init-sensitivity width="90%"}

As shown in @fig-init-sensitivity, **the influence of initial parameter values differed substantially across transmission-pathway profiles**. Under the baseline profile, parameter estimates were generally close to the true SI values across initialization strategies. The mean-misspecified and ICC-based starts produced nearly identical mean estimates, averaging approximately 15.07 days. However, the SD-misspecified strategy occasionally produced markedly underestimated means, indicating that the baseline profile was not entirely insensitive to initialization.

The CP-heavy profile in @fig-init-sensitivity exhibited a much stronger dependence on the initial SD. When the true SD was supplied, the mean-misspecified start produced estimates close to the target distribution for most repetitions, with an average estimated SI mean of approximately 15.82 days. In contrast, the SD-misspecified and ICC-based strategies consistently produced substantial underestimation, with average estimated means of approximately 3.26 days, corresponding to a bias of $-11.74$ days. These inaccurate solutions were accompanied by pronounced deviations in the fitted pathway weights: the estimated CP weight approached zero, while the PQ weight increased to approximately 0.79, compared with its true value of 0.10. Notably, all runs under these two initialization strategies satisfied the numerical convergence criterion despite the substantial estimation bias.

A different pattern was observed for the higher-generation-heavy profile in @fig-init-sensitivity, where both the initial mean and SD affected parameter recovery. Replacing the initial mean with the ICC sample mean resulted in an average estimate of approximately 29.93 days, even when the initial SD remained correctly specified. The SD-misspecified strategy produced an intermediate average of approximately 23.05 days, with final estimates concentrated in distinct regions near the true value and at substantially higher values. When both parameters were initialized using ICC sample moments, the estimated mean increased to approximately 29.62 days. These results suggest that the higher-generation-heavy profile was sensitive to both initial parameters, rather than predominantly to the initial SD.

Comparisons across pathway profiles in @fig-init-sensitivity further illustrate that the effect of misspecification was not uniform. Mean misspecification had little effect on final estimates under the baseline and CP-heavy profiles but was associated with substantial overestimation under the higher-generation-heavy profile. Conversely, SD misspecification was particularly detrimental under the CP-heavy profile and produced less consistent outcomes under the other profiles. The ICC-based strategy performed well under the baseline profile but resulted in substantial biases under both alternative pathway compositions. Thus, the results indicate that the sensitivity of the estimation procedure to initialization is closely associated with the underlying pathway composition.

Initialization also influenced computational behaviour in @fig-init-sensitivity. Under the CP-heavy profile, median EM iterations increased from approximately 16–17 when the true SD was supplied to approximately 97–99 when using the ICC-derived SD. Similarly, under the higher-generation-heavy profile, the ICC-based start had a median iteration count of 66. These differences suggest that less suitable starting values may lead to slower stabilization, even when the algorithm eventually satisfies its convergence criterion.

Overall, @fig-init-sensitivity provides evidence that inaccurate parameter recovery under low dispersion can, at least partly, be associated with the initialization of the EM algorithm. In particular, changing the initial parameters substantially improved estimation accuracy under the CP-heavy and higher-generation-heavy profiles, demonstrating that the large biases observed in the main simulation were not inevitable under those pathway compositions. Nevertheless, the analysis was restricted to the low-dispersion setting and should be interpreted as a preliminary investigation of initialization sensitivity rather than a comprehensive assessment across all underlying SI distributions.


### C.5 Sensitivity to the EM Iteration Cap

To assess the effect of the iteration limit, an additional diagnostic was conducted under the baseline pathway ($N=100$), allowing up to 2,000 EM iterations for moderate- and high-dispersion scenarios, with 100 repetitions each.

As shown in @fig-iteration-cap-diagnostic, 96% and 99% of repetitions converged within 2,000 iterations under moderate and high dispersion, respectively. While many fits converged within the first few hundred iterations, some required substantially more. This suggests that increasing the iteration cap can improve convergence at the expense of additional computation. The 300-iteration limit was therefore adopted as a pragmatic computational trade-off for the main simulation.
